\section{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}
% 2026-09-21 house shape: four setup blocks, Exp-N paragraphs (pointer -> axis -> headline -> highlight -> anomaly), case studies
% continue the numbering; no subsections; monochrome figures (ours black, STrees grey); short captions.  Numbers: tables/*.tex
% generated by make_tables.py from the records, macros in tables/*_stats.tex; case-study numbers from case/*.json.

\stitle{Hardware.}
All code is C++23, single-threaded, compiled with \texttt{-O3}.
%
We use a laptop (Apple M-series) and two Ubuntu 22.04 servers (GCC 11.4, 96 cores, 503~GB of memory).
%
No timing run of ours shared a machine with another timing run of ours.
%
The servers carried a background load of 1 to 8 from other users.
%
Laptop and server latencies are not directly comparable, since the servers' single-core speed is 1.5 to 3 times lower; every table names its machine.

\stitle{Algorithms.}
\chainidx is the index of Sections~\ref{sec:index} to~\ref{sec:construction}, built by \build and queried by \query.
%
\strees is the index of Section~\ref{sec:strees}, one tree and one DFS array per size with every value stored.
%
Its size is computed from the same decomposition.
%
Its query latency is measured by our own implementation, built in the same process from the same decomposition and run on the same queries.
%
\cnd is the published counting-based nucleus decomposition~\cite{Zhang2026NucleusCounting}, run once per size with its default settings.
%
It computes core values only, and it competes on construction and not on storage.
%
The implementation of \chainidx was checked against brute force on $34{,}075$ graphs.
%
These are every labelled graph on at most six vertices, 200 random graphs on 7 to 10 vertices, split graphs, $K_8$ and $K_{300}$.
%
Every $(v,s,k)$ was queried in four storage forms, under a release build and under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.
%
On the real graphs the number of canonical nodes agrees with an independent implementation.
%
The index of a graph is byte-identical across the two servers even when the input files list the edges in different orders.

\stitle{Datasets.}
We use \numgraphs{} real graphs from five families.
%
They are collaboration graphs (\textsf{ca-*}, \textsf{com-dblp}, \textsf{dblp-*}), citation graphs (\textsf{cit-*}), web graphs (\textsf{web-*}), product co-purchase graphs (\textsf{amazon*}, \textsf{com-amazon}), and social and communication networks (\textsf{soc-*}, \textsf{com-youtube}, \textsf{email-Eu-core}, \textsf{wiki-Talk}, \textsf{loc-Brightkite}, \textsf{tech-as-skitter}).
%
They range from $1{,}005$ to $4{,}049{,}537$ vertices, with largest cliques from $7$ to $500$ vertices; Table~\ref{tab:size} lists them with their number of sizes $s_{\max}$.
%
Three larger graphs, \textsf{com-lj}, \textsf{ca-hollywood-2009} and \textsf{com-orkut}, exhaust the 503~GB of the server inside the clique tree of the peel.
%
They have no index yet.

\stitle{Metrics.}
Queries are drawn from the vertices with $\omg{v}\ge2$ and their sizes $2\le s\le\omg{v}$.
%
The workload has $20{,}000$ community queries at the vertex's own level ($k=\core{s}{v}$), $20{,}000$ at half that level, $1{,}000$ at $k=1$, and $200{,}000$ value queries.
%
Every latency is the per-query average of the median of five passes after one warm-up pass.
%
Sizes are bytes of the structure in memory; build times exclude the reading of the graph.
%
Every number in the tables and figures is generated from the recorded measurements.

\expsection{Index size}
Table~\ref{tab:size} lists every graph with its number of chains, its vertices per chain and its share of values stored explicitly.
%
The next two columns are the sizes of \chainidx and of \strees.
%
The last column is the ratio of the two sizes.
%
\chainidx is \ratiomin$\times$ to \ratiomax$\times$ smaller than \strees, median \ratiomedian$\times$.
%
The ratio follows the vertices per chain.
%
\emailcore, with $1{,}005$ vertices in $667$ chains, is the worst case at \ratiomin$\times$.
%
\webuk, with $129{,}632$ vertices in $839$ chains and cliques of $500$ vertices, is the best at \ratiomax$\times$.
%
The two coauthorship graphs with the largest cliques compress by $45.8\times$ and $12.0\times$.
%
The web graphs compress by $5.7\times$ to $48.7\times$, and the social graphs by $2.9\times$ to $15.9\times$.
%
If the graph is not stored in the index's order, the label permutation adds $4n$ bytes and lowers the ratios to \permmin$\times$ to \permmax$\times$ (median \permmedian$\times$).

\expsection{Where the bytes go}
On the collaboration, web and product graphs the per-size trees with their run arrays are $58$ to $74$ percent of the index.
%
The chain records are $23$ to $41$ percent.
%
On the social and citation graphs, where chains are shorter, the chain records reach $44$ to $58$ percent.
%
Most of it is the trajectories, one node id per chain and size.
%
The map is $3$ to $13$ percent.
%
The values are a small part everywhere once residues and per-size widths are in place.
%
The certified tail (Theorem~\ref{thm:tail}) is what makes them small.
%
The share of active (vertex, size) pairs whose value must be stored ranges from \storedmin{} percent to \storedmax{} percent, with a median of \storedmedian{} percent (Table~\ref{tab:size}).
%
On \webuk one residue serves $23.5$ million pairs; \emailcore is the other end.
%
The share is lowest on the graphs with large cliques, where most of a vertex's values lie in its tail.
%
It is highest on the sparse social and citation graphs, where $\sigma$ is close to $\omega$.

\expsection{Design study}
Table~\ref{tab:layouts} isolates the layout decisions on five graphs.
%
Each column is one layout, and each row the bytes it takes on one graph.
%
Trees over twin classes do not help, since twin classes have $1.03$ to $1.28$ vertices.
%
Trees over chains with an explicit vertex-to-chain map are $2.5\times$ to $4.5\times$ smaller than \strees.
%
Aligned labels remove the map and turn answers into ranges, and run arrays with entry points and per-size widths give the final sizes.
%
We also implemented the skyline deduplication of SGL~\cite{SGL} over chains.
%
It was $0.99\times$ to $2.28\times$ smaller than the corresponding tree layout but $2$ to $3$ times slower to query.
%
It is not part of the index.

\expsection{Query latency}
Table~\ref{tab:queries} reports the own-level community query and the value query.
%
The community columns are the time to locate a community, the number of ranges of the answer, its size, and the time to list it as vertex labels.
%
Beside the two community times stand those of \strees on the same queries.
%
Locating takes \locmin{} to \locmax{}~ns, median \locmedian{}~ns.
%
A community of $1.9$ million vertices on the $4$-million-vertex coauthorship graph is located in $11$~ns and listed in $167~\mu$s.
%
At the own level \strees locates in about \stlocown{} of that time.
%
Its own-node lookup is two dependent loads, against the map, trajectory and entry reads of \chainidx.
%
Listing costs \pervmin{} to \pervmax{}~ns per vertex on the graphs whose mean answer has at least a thousand vertices.
%
On the two graphs with answers below a hundred vertices the fixed cost of a query dominates.
%
Against the memory copy of \strees, the listing time of \chainidx ranges from \stmin$\times$ to \stmax$\times$ (median \stmedian), faster on \stfaster{} of the \stpoints{} (graph, level) points.
%
A run costs eight bytes to read however many labels it expands to.
%
\chainidx is therefore faster where the answer is a few long ranges, on the social, product and web graphs.
%
It is slower where the answer is fragmented.
%
\emailcore, \textsf{cit-HepPh} and \textsf{ca-AstroPh} have $2$ to $5$ vertices per range, and there one range costs as much as tens of copied labels.
%
Value queries take \valmin{} to \valmax{}~ns, median \valmedian{}~ns.
%
The slowest is \webuk, whose binomial table for cliques of $500$ vertices no longer fits the first-level cache.

Figure~\ref{fig:regimes} shows the three levels of the workload for both indexes.
%
The left panel plots the listing time against the mean size of the answer, one point per graph and level.
%
The right panel plots the locating time by level.
%
Listing time is linear in the size of the answer at every level, for \chainidx and for the copy alike.
%
It lies between $0.05$ and $0.5$~ns per vertex above a fixed cost of a few nanoseconds.
%
Locating costs a median of \ownmedian{}~ns at the own level, \halfmedian{}~ns at half the level and \rootmedian{}~ns at $k=1$.
%
The jump pointers make the climb to the root as cheap as no climb at all.
%
The half-level climb stops at an interior node and costs at most \halfmax{}~ns.
%
The parent-pointer climb of \strees has no such bound.
%
At the two deeper levels it costs up to \stlocdeepmax$\times$ the time of \chainidx.
%
On the coauthorship graph, whose hierarchy has $5{,}543$ levels, the half level takes $1{,}086$~ns against $109$~ns.

\end{figure*}

\expsection{Latency by clique size and by answer size}
Figure~\ref{fig:profile} separates the two variables that the mixed workload averages, on the four largest graphs of the second server.
%
Panel (a) plots the locating time against the clique size, and panel (b) the listing time against the clique size.
%
Panel (c) plots the listing time against the answer size.
%
Solid lines are \chainidx and dashed lines \strees.
%
Panels (a) and (b) draw $5{,}000$ own-level queries per clique size, the vertex uniform among the vertices active at that size.
%
\chainidx locates in $8$ to $44$~ns at every size, highest at $s=4$ to $6$ where the per-size trees have the most nodes.
%
\strees locates in $2$ to $11$~ns.
%
At $s=2$ and $3$, where the answers are large and consist of a few long runs, \chainidx lists $1.0\times$ to $3.2\times$ faster than the memory copy.
%
From $s=4$ on, where the own-level answers shrink to hundreds or a few thousand vertices spread over many ranges, the copy is $2\times$ to $5\times$ faster.
%
Panel (c) sorts the $20{,}000$ own-level queries of the fixed workload by answer size into deciles.
%
Below $10^5$ vertices the copy is $2\times$ to $3\times$ faster, and above it the two coincide within $10$ percent.
%
\chainidx trades a constant per range for a constant per label; the bytes it saves (Table~\ref{tab:size}) do not depend on the answer.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_profile.pdf}

\end{figure*}

\expsection{Scalability}
Figure~\ref{fig:scale} follows \textsf{cit-Patents} and \textsf{web-BerkStan} through vertex-induced random samples of $20$, $40$, $60$ and $80$ percent of their vertices up to the full graph.
%
The runs are on the second server.
%
The x-axis is the number of vertices.
%
The panels show the bytes of both indexes, then the build time of \chainidx and of \cnd run once per size, then the own-level locating and listing time of both indexes.
%
A sample keeps about the square of the fraction of the edges.
%
The curves therefore show a graph family growing in size and in density at once; the largest cliques of \textsf{web-BerkStan} go from $45$ to $202$ vertices.
%
\chainidx grows about linearly with the vertices, $2.9$ to $3.2$ bytes per vertex on \textsf{cit-Patents} and $5.3$ to $12.6$ on \textsf{web-BerkStan} as its cliques grow.
%
\strees grows with the vertices times the sizes they take part in.
%
The ratio rises along each curve, from $7.7\times$ to $12.1\times$ and from $6.4\times$ to $19.2\times$.
%
The build grows faster than the graph: $0.56$ to $19.5$ seconds over five times the vertices of \textsf{cit-Patents}, and $0.21$ to $65.6$ seconds on \textsf{web-BerkStan}.
%
\cnd once per size grows faster still.
%
Its ratio to the build of \chainidx rises from $6.6\times$ to $18\times$ along the \textsf{cit-Patents} curve and lies between $61\times$ and $135\times$ along the \textsf{web-BerkStan} curve.
%
Query latency does not move: locating stays between $21$ and $28$~ns and listing between $0.09$ and $0.21$~ns per vertex at every size.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_scale.pdf}
\caption{Vary graph size.}\label{fig:scale}
\end{figure*}

\expsection{Against one decomposition per size}
\cnd computes the $(1,s)$ core values of one size per run.
%
Obtaining every size with it means one run per size.
%
Table~\ref{tab:prior} sums those runs over $s=2,\dots,s_{\max}$ on \priorgraphs{} (graph, machine) pairs.
%
It reports the whole-process wall time and the in-process build and peel timers alone, against the whole build of \chainidx on the same machine.
%
Counting only the clique-tree build and peel of \cnd, \chainidx is built \priormin$\times$ (com-amazon, six sizes) to \priormax$\times$ (\webuk, $499$ sizes) faster, median \priormedian$\times$.
%
Counting the whole processes of \cnd, which reload and sort the graph for every size, the factors are larger still.
%
The clique tree is built once instead of once per size.
%
The sizes share their peel through the certificate of Theorem~\ref{thm:replay} and the Kruskal--Katona cap.
%
The ratio grows with the number of sizes.
%
On \textsf{web-BerkStan} ($201$ sizes) the $2.3$ hours of \cnd become $66$ seconds, and on \webuk{} $15.7$ hours become $70$ seconds.
%
The same table is the cost of answering a community query without an index.
%
The smallest possible online answer is one decomposition at the queried size, seconds to minutes per query on these graphs, against the nanoseconds of Table~\ref{tab:queries}.

\expsection{Case Study I: the best size varies per query}
We study which clique size best recovers ground-truth communities.
%
Three SNAP graphs come with them: \dblp (publication venues), \textsf{com-amazon} (product categories) and \textsf{com-youtube} (user groups), the top $5{,}000$ communities of each.
%
Take a member $v$ of a ground-truth community $C$.
%
For every size $s\le\omg{v}$ and every level $k$, we score the $(s,k)$-nucleus of $v$ by its F1 against $C$.
%
The whole $(s,k)$ space of a query is scanned from the index without listing a community.
%
$|N\cap C|$ is counted through the members of $C$, whose own nodes fall inside the node's subtree or not, and $|N|$ comes from the run bounds.
%
The absolute scale of $k$ differs between sizes, and we compare the best level of each size.
%
The $k$-core index is size $2$ at its best level.
%
Table~\ref{tab:casegt} compares four choices: the $k$-core index, the triangle size at its best level, the best single size for the graph, and the best size or (size, level) chosen per query.
%
Table~\ref{tab:casehist} gives where the best size falls.
%
\sstitle{No single size is right on \dblp.}
The best size spreads over $2$ to $8$.
%
$26$ percent of the queries are best served at size $2$, $23$ at $3$, $18$ at $4$, $13$ at $5$ and $20$ at $6$ or more.
%
Choosing the size per query gives an F1 of $0.179$, $3.6\times$ the $0.049$ of the $k$-core index and $1.2\times$ the $0.140$ of the best fixed size.
%
For $74$ percent of the queries some size other than $2$ beats every $k$-core.
%
\sstitle{One size can be enough.}
On \textsf{com-amazon} the triangle size alone reaches $0.824$ against $0.851$ for the per-query choice, and both are $1.8\times$ the $k$-core index.
%
On \textsf{com-youtube} every cohesive model is far from the ground-truth groups, with F1 below $0.04$, a known property of that dataset.
%
The comparison says nothing there.
%
\sstitle{The choice is cheap with the index.}
The per-query scan over every size and level costs $1$ to $50~\mu$s from \chainidx.
%
Without the index, each size of the scan would be one decomposition of the graph.

\expsection{Case Study II: the size as a zoom on Amazon}
We study \textsf{com-amazon} joined with the SNAP product metadata, titles, groups and category paths, which covers $334{,}852$ of its $334{,}863$ products.
%
For a query product $q$, the \textit{leaf purity} of a community is the share of its members that share a leaf category with $q$.
%
Its \textit{subject purity} is the share that share a subject with $q$.
%
A subject is the third level of the category tree, such as Jazz, Computers \& Internet or Science Fiction \& Fantasy.
%
Table~\ref{tab:caseamazon} follows $5{,}000$ products, drawn uniformly among those active at size $3$, through their own-level community at every size.
%
\sstitle{Purity rises and size falls with the clique size.}
At size $2$, the $k$-core, three quarters of the products sit in one core of $157{,}331$ products at $10$ percent leaf purity.
%
Size $3$ brings the median community to $38$ products at $44$ percent.
%
Size $4$ brings it to $11$ products at $70$ percent, and size $5$ to $8$ products at $79$ percent.
%
From size $4$ on, the community's dominant subject covers $99$ percent of its members.
%
\sstitle{The communities read as shelves.}
Table~\ref{tab:caseexamples} lists six products.
%
``Kind of Blue'' goes from $36{,}878$ products ($1$ percent jazz) at size $2$ to $23$ Blue Note albums at size $3$.
%
At size $5$ it is six albums, the canonical jazz shelf.
%
``Introduction to Algorithms'' goes from the $157{,}331$-product core to $57$ computing books at size $3$ and $13$ theory textbooks at size $4$.
%
The Godfather soundtrack reaches $28$ products at size $5$ whose category purity is only $0.32$.
%
They are one shelf all the same: the four soundtracks with Jerry Vale, Lou Monte and ``Italian American Classics''.
%
The category tree has no name for this community.
%
\sstitle{Practical guideline.}
Size $3$ is the first size at which most communities become readable, and sizes $4$ and $5$ isolate the shelf.
%
Every community after size $2$ is a handful of ranges and is listed in under $50$~ns.
